End of Life Doula

By: Tarryn Crossman | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
As it becomes a growing trend in South Africa we ask what is an End of Life Doula?

Summary:
An end of Life/Death Doula is not a medical professional, their primary role is to emotionally support the dying and their family. The Doula explains it as, “Helping the patient to live while dying”. Practically they help with legacy projects, closing lose ends with loved ones, confronting the fear of dying and what happens next. Often when someone are passing their main concern is the well being of those they are leaving behind, the job of an end of life Doula is to allow them the space to speak about their own fears and unfinished business.

Further information:
Specialist 1
Samala was a birthing Doula until she was working with a woman who lost her baby at 39 weeks. During the process of this birth she realised that the support for families who lose babies is just not there. Woman are never given the chance to celebrate their child's little lives and say goodbye with love and respect. So she did an online American course and started end of life Doula’ing for pediatrics.

She says the difference her clients experience by having her is profound. She births the babies with them as if they were still alive and then they get to hold their babies and say goodbye. She also does post birth counselling at the families homes and helps them organize their own version of a funeral or memorial.
If a baby is medically terminated under 26 weeks it is considered medical waste, so she also organizes the affidavits needed to have the body buried or cremated according to the families wishes

The support is just not there for women who have miscarriages or have to face their child's mortality before it is even born. For many reasons, one of which is the shame that woman feel around failing their child and their partners. This is where Samala’s role as an end of life Doula becomes crucial. Supporting both the mother and the father to celebrate and grieve their child with dignity.

Case study options
Samala is working with a woman who has just be told her baby in womb is terminally ill, so she is speaking to her about letting us document their sessions together
Alternatively
She has a couple that she worked with at the end of last year that would be willing to tell their story.



Specialist 2 – CT based, but has a case study for us
Well spoken and excited about sharing her story
Denny first supported someone in the last days when she was 13 years old. Her nanny at the time was dying and she sat with her until the end. She then went on to support her parents and finally friends and strangers. Being an end of life Doula is a calling for her, it was never about money.
There is no local End of life Doula training as yet, so Denny was operating off her experience as a social worker. But she has now completed a 5-week training with hospice.

Case study option
Denny is busy counselling Rosie, she is in her 60’s and has been diagnosed with a rear and terminal blood disease. Rosie has agreed to allow us to film her counselling sessions and her personal life etc.

Specialist 3 – JHB based, but no case study yet
Stasha is a birth doula and an end of life Doula she has many more years of experience than Denny and is such an amazing character. Warm, spiritual, articulate and smart. She says she can get back to me tomorrow about a case study

Specialist 4 – we don’t necessarily need her if we use Denny, as Denny can talk about the training Nicci does
Nicci is also a Doula, but for Pediatrics and she isn’t as strong a character as Samala. She is working with DOSA, Doula’s of South Africa, to create the first South Africa End of Life Doula training. It will also be online, but in comparison to the 5-11 000$ it costs to do the American course it will only cost R3000

One CT specialist and Case study

Time code CHARACTER / VISUAL
1 00:00 Voice over Death is not something we are ever really taught how to cope with, but the
use of a death doula is increasing in South Africa and changing this isolating
space
2 00:09 Odette They say that grief is love that is unexpressed so it’s the love that you can’t pass over any more. It sits inside and you don’t know what to do with it because you have all this love and you can’t give it. Part of a sitting vigil is being able to say to the family express your love now, the time is coming
3 00:30 Claire link The fact that we are born and that we will die are the only definite in life yes as human beings we have an overwhelming fear of death that often makes us feel very alone in those final hours which is where a death doula comes in.
4 00:47 Voice over Samala initially trained as a birthing Doula, but after one of her mom’s lost
their baby at 37 weeks, the grief process and lack of support for the family
inspired her journey in becoming a death Doula
5 01:00 Samala and Claire Samala: A doula is a woman who saves, it’s a Greek word for a woman who saves, and as a doula we serve in different situations. So, we have a birth doula, she will serve in pregnancy, labour and birth.
6 01:14 Mother giving birth
7 01:18 Samala We are there for the emotional support then we also have a bereavement doula or death doula. I also serve as a bereavement doula in baby loss. There is such a sacredness in birth but there’s also an incredibly deep sacredness in death and in passing. And we try and create that safe space for that family to find their way to honour their baby in the way they need to, and to experience the beauty and the spirituality of saying goodbye to their little person
8 01:55 Voice over Samala worked with Nicolette during the loss of her baby at 24 weeks
9 01:59 Nicolette and Claire interview Nicolette: It was a difficult pregnancy and you just felt this anxiety. From about 14 weeks I struggled with the urinary traction infection. I woke up in the middle of the night and realised my water just broken so I came straight to the hospital and they took me immediately and I spent 3 weeks in bed rest. The baby was fine still, there was 50/50% chance and my membrane could heal again.

Claire: And so, what happened near the end of that 3 weeks?

Nicolette: I went into labour and my little girl was born. Unfortunately, she was still born and that was exactly at 24 weeks.

Claire: that must be every mother’s worse night mare

Nicolette: nothing could prepare you for that. it’s really devastating.
10 02:48 Voice over Odette is a death doula that works with Adults and the families that are left
behind after someone passes. She is working with a cancer patient who wishes to remain anonymous.
11 02:59 Odette What the work entails is being a complete support system for the terminally ill patient. You go shopping together, you go for walks in the garden, you touch, you support, you hold hands, you talk, you find out what they want and what they don’t want. Assisting them putting together a life book, like a memoirs book, history book, things that a terminally ill patient wants to remember. Grandchildren to remember. The death doula or end of life doula sets all of that stuff in place with the family so that the patient gets what they need as they are approaching their end of life.
12 03:40 Odette and patient Odette: Speak your truth.

Patient: I think there’s a fear of dying

Odette: is it fear of what’s on the other side? Is it fearing of leaving?

Patient: I’m not sure I think its maybe a life unfulfilled.
13 03:56 Voice over Apart of what a death doula does is help a family with logistics so that they
can focus on grieving. Because Nicolette lost her baby at 24 weeks Samala
had to organise an affidavit for her to keep Alexia’s body after she passed
14 04:12 Samala and Claire interview Samala: in South Africa, we have a law that says pre-26 weeks any baby that’s born and doesn’t take a breath is considered premedical waste and so they are incinerated in the hospital with medical waste. So as bereavement doulas there is a death certificate we can help to get those little babies to a funeral home so that mom and dad can have a funeral or a cremation. Which is hugely important for their healing a growth journey and their grieving because otherwise they don’t find that closure very often
15 04:50 Nicolette I had the option of meeting alexia the following day and that is when Samala came to see me and she helped me to prepare a little emotionally to meet alexia and Samala actually went a dressed her and they wrapped her in a little blanket and put a beanie on and when I finally went to meet her she looked really beautiful and peaceful, Samala arranged for a photographer to come in and take photos of alexia
16 05:18 Voice over Samala highly encourages all her families to take photos with their babies
after they have passed.
17 05:24 Samala 9 out of 10 times when we discuss taking photos with mom and dad the reaction is oh I don’t know if I want that. but having worked with couples and mommies and support groups the number one regret that couples have is not having photos or not having enough photos.
18 05:43 Nicolette It was a beautiful experience in the end that we will always treasure, and those are the only memories we have.
19 05:50 Voice over A death Doula will sit vigil with a patient and their family guiding them through
the dying process, until the person passes
20 06:00 Odette The benefits of just sitting at a bed side and holding somebody’s hand and acknowledging that they are still there and that the process that they are going through is a natural one and its okay to be like that and that person becomes valued and everything that they had in their lives up until that moment has meaning and when somebody is dying and you can feel their story is important they can pass with peace, and end of life doula that’s your purpose, to bridge the gap between this living world and world that comes here you after.
21 06:40 Claire link A death doula gives control to the people that are dying. They help patients transition on their own terms
22 06:49 Nicolette If I didn’t have a bereavement doula I wouldn’t have known that I would meet my baby and that they experience would've been very cold and so having a bereavement doula there has really soften the process and really made it a memory more than something I wouldn’t want to look back on.
23 07:07 Voice over Death Douling is not an entirely new idea, people have been supporting each other through death for many generations but it is a new word for an old concept that is brining death back into mainstream dialogue
24 07:20 Odette If we go back to the late 1800’s early 1900’s death was very much part of how communities functioned. Death was not something that was shoved to the side “shh shh can’t talk about it” and as we have evolved as a society, death has become shh shh we can’t talk about that. so, end of life doulas are working incredibly hard to bring death back into our everyday lives and when they are terminal they are not isolated or alone they are part of a community and that community supports them through their process of dying
